p.src: As Lin Daiyu stood lost in a web of tender, lingering thoughts, someone suddenly slapped her on the back and asked, “What are you doing here all by yourself?” Lin Daiyu started in fright and turned around; it was none other than Xiangling. “You silly girl!” said Lin Daiyu. “What a fright you gave me. Where have you come from just now?” Xiangling giggled. “I came looking for our young mistress, but I can’t find her anywhere. Your Zijuan is looking for you too. She says Second Mistress Lian has sent you some tea. Come, let’s go home and sit down.” As she spoke, she took Daiyu by the hand and led her back to the潇湘館. Sure enough, Xifeng had sent two small jars of newly harvested tribute tea. Lin Daiyu and Xiangling sat down together. They had no serious business to discuss, of course: they merely admired how well one piece had been embroidered and how finely another had been worked, played a game of chess, and read a few lines from a book; then Xiangling left. No more need be said of that.

p.src: Let us now return to Baoyu. After Xiren had fetched him back to his room, he found Yuanyang reclining on the bed, examining Xiren’s needlework. Seeing him enter, she said, “Where have you been? The Old Lady is waiting for you. She wants you to go over and pay your respects to the First Master. Hurry and change your clothes, then be off.” Xiren went into the inner room to fetch his clothes. Baoyu sat on the edge of the bed, slipped off his shoes, and waited for his boots. Turning, he saw Yuanyang in a pale-red figured-silk jacket and a blue satin vest, with a white crêpe-silk sash about her waist. Her face was turned away and her head bent over the needlework, while a flowered collar encircled her neck. Baoyu pressed his face close to her neck to breathe in the scent of her hair oil and kept stroking skin as fair and smooth as Xiren’s. Clambering against her, he grinned impudently and said, “Dear sister, let me taste the rouge on your lips.” As he spoke, he clung to her like a twisted stick of candy. Yuanyang cried, “Xiren, come out and look at him! You’ll be with him all your life—why don’t you admonish him? He still behaves like this!” Xiren came out carrying the clothes and said to Baoyu, “No matter how often I admonish you, you never change. Just what are we to do with you? If you carry on like this, it will become impossible for us to remain here.” As she spoke, she hurried him into his clothes; then he and Yuanyang went to the front apartments to see Grandmother Jia.

If you carry on like this, it will become impossible for us to remain here.”
As she spoke, she hurried him into his clothes; then he and Yuanyang went to the front apartments to see Grandmother Jia.

p.src: After seeing Grandmother Jia, Baoyu went outside, where attendants and horses were already waiting. Just as he was about to mount, Jia Lian returned from paying his respects and was dismounting. The two met face-to-face and exchanged a few words. Then a man stepped out from the side and said, “My respects to Uncle Bao.” Baoyu looked at him. He had a long face and a tall, slender figure and appeared only eighteen or nineteen. He was refined and decidedly handsome, and his face seemed very familiar; yet Baoyu could not recall which branch of the family he belonged to or what his name was. Jia Lian laughed. “Why are you staring blankly? Don’t you even recognize him? He is Yun, the son of Fifth Sister-in-law, who lives by the rear gallery.” “Of course, of course,” said Baoyu with a laugh. “How could I have forgotten?” He asked after Jia Yun’s mother and inquired what business had brought him there. Pointing at Jia Lian, Jia Yun replied, “I came to speak with Second Uncle.” Baoyu laughed. “You have grown even more distinguished-looking than before. You could almost be my son.” “Have you no shame?” laughed Jia Lian. He is four or five years older than you, and you would make him your son?” Baoyu laughed. “How old are you this year?” “Eighteen,” replied Jia Yun.

p.src: Now Jia Yun was exceedingly quick-witted and perceptive. Hearing Baoyu’s remark, he laughed and said, “As the proverb goes, ‘A grandfather may lie in a cradle, and his grandson walk with a cane.’ Though I may be older, no mountain rises higher than the sun. Since my father died, there has been no one to look after or instruct me all these years. If Uncle Bao does not despise your nephew for his foolishness and will acknowledge me as his son, it would be my great good fortune.” Jia Lian laughed. “Did you hear that? Acknowledging a son is no simple matter!” With that, he went inside. Baoyu said with a smile, “Come and see me whenever you are free tomorrow; don’t skulk about with those others. I have no time just now. Come to my study tomorrow. We can chat about everything under the sun, and I’ll take you into the garden to amuse ourselves.” So saying, he seized the saddle and mounted, then rode toward Jia She’s residence surrounded by his young attendants.

p.src: When he saw Jia She, it proved to be no more than a slight chill. Baoyu first conveyed Grandmother Jia’s inquiries and then paid his own respects. Jia She first rose and made his reply to Grandmother Jia; then he summoned a servant. “Take the young master inside to sit with the mistress.” Baoyu withdrew, went to the rear apartments, and entered the principal room. When Lady Xing saw him arrive, she rose first and asked after Grandmother Jia; only then did Baoyu pay his respects to her. Lady Xing drew him onto the kang beside her, asked after the others, and ordered tea to be served. Before he had finished one cup of tea, Jia Cong came in to pay his respects to Baoyu. Lady Xing exclaimed, “Where have you been playing the wild monkey? Are all your nurses dead, that none of them tidies you up? With those black brows and that filthy mouth, you hardly look like the studious son of a great family!” While she was speaking, Jia Huan and his young nephew Jia Lan also arrived. After paying their respects, Lady Xing told them both to sit on chairs. Seeing Baoyu share Lady Xing’s cushion while she caressed and fussed over him in every way, Jia Huan had long since begun to feel resentful. Before they had sat there long, he signalled to Jia Lan that he wanted to leave. Jia Lan had no choice but to comply, and the two rose together to take their leave. Seeing that they were leaving, Baoyu also rose, intending to return with them. Lady Xing smiled. “Stay seated for a while. I still have something to say to you.” Baoyu had no choice but to sit down again. Lady Xing said to the other two, “When you go back, each of you give my regards to your mother. Your girl cousins and all your elder and younger sisters are here, and their commotion has made my head spin, so I shall not keep you for dinner today.” Jia Huan and the others assented, went out, and returned home.

p.src: Baoyu smiled and said, “But haven’t all my cousins come over? Why haven’t I seen them?” Lady Xing replied, “They sat here for a while, then went off somewhere in the back—I don’t know which room.” Baoyu said, “Aunt, you said just now that you had something to tell me. What was it?” Lady Xing laughed. “What could I have to say? I merely wanted you to wait and have dinner with your sisters before you leave. And I have an amusing little thing for you to take home and play with.” As aunt and nephew talked, before they knew it the hour for the evening meal had arrived. Tables and chairs were arranged and cups and dishes set out; the ladies and girls finished their meal together. Baoyu went to take leave of Jia She, then returned home with his sisters. After paying their respects to Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, and the others, they each retired to their rooms to rest. No more need be said of this. Now Jia Yun went in to see Jia Lian and asked whether any work was available. Jia Lian told him, “A job did come up the other day, but your aunt kept begging me for it, so I gave it to Jia Qin. He has assured me that several more places in the garden will need flowers and trees planted tomorrow. When that work is commissioned, I shall certainly give it to you.” Jia Yun listened and, after a long silence, said, “In that case, I shall wait. Uncle, there is no need to mention to Aunt yet that I came today to inquire about it. It will not be too late to tell her when the time comes.” Jia Lian replied, “Why should I mention it to her? Where would I find the time for such idle talk? Tomorrow at the fifth watch I must make a trip to Xingyi, and I must return the same day. Go and wait for now. Come for news the day after tomorrow, sometime after the watch begins; if you come too early, I shall not be free.” With that, he went into the rear apartments to change his clothes.

p.src: Jia Yun left the Rongguo Mansion and headed home. Pondering all the way, he devised a plan and went straight to the house of his maternal uncle, Bu Shiren. Bu Shiren kept a spice shop and had only just returned from it. When Jia Yun unexpectedly came in, they exchanged greetings, and Bu Shiren asked what had brought him there at such an hour. Jia Yun said, “There is something for which I need your help, Uncle. I have a use for some borneol and musk. Whatever you can do, please let me have four taels of each on credit, and in the eighth month I shall bring you the full amount in silver.” Bu Shiren sneered. “Say no more about buying on credit. Not long ago, one of the assistants in our shop let a relative have several taels’ worth of goods on credit, and the debt has still not been repaid. We all had to bear the loss, so we drew up an agreement that no one would ever again extend credit to relatives or friends. Anyone who does so must pay twenty taels of silver to treat the rest of us. Besides, those goods are scarce just now. Even if you brought ready silver to buy them at our wretched little shop, we would not have that much; you would have to try elsewhere. That is my first reason. Second, what proper business could you possibly have? You would merely take the goods on credit and squander them on some foolishness. You always claim that whenever your uncle sees you, he finds fault with you. But you young people have no sense of what is good for you. If only you would make some firm plan, earn a little money, and provide yourself properly with food and clothing, I too would be glad to see it.”

p.src: Jia Yun smiled. “Uncle, you make it sound very simple. When my father died, I was still too young to understand anything. Later, I heard from my mother that it was thanks to you uncles coming to our house, advising us, and arranging the funeral that we managed at all. Surely you know whether there was so much as an acre of land or a couple of rooms left for me to squander away? Even the cleverest housewife cannot make porridge without rice. What would you have me do? You should be thankful that it is only I. Were it someone else, he would brazenly pester you every few days for three measures of rice or two of beans, and then even you would be at your wits’ end.”

p.src: Bu Shiren said, “My boy, if your uncle had the means, of course he ought to help you. I tell your aunt every day that my only worry is that you have no plan for making your way. If you had any enterprise, you would go to the senior branch of the family; even if you could not see the masters themselves, you could humble yourself and cultivate their stewards or managers until they found you some business to oversee. The other day, on my way out of the city, I met Fourth Master from your third branch riding a big jackass, with five carts and forty or fifty Buddhist and Taoist monks, all bound for the family temple. He certainly knows how to get things done—that whole affair has been entrusted to him!” Jia Yun could bear no more of his uncle’s endless prattle and rose to take his leave. “Why are you in such a hurry?” said Bu Shiren. “Stay and eat before you go.” Before he had finished, his wife broke in: “You are being foolish again. You just said there was no rice, so I bought half a catty of flour to make noodles for you, and now you are putting on airs of abundance. Would you keep your nephew here only to let him go hungry?” “Then buy another half-catty and add it to the pot,” said Bu Shiren. His wife called to their daughter: “Yinjie, go across to Granny Wang’s and ask whether she can lend us twenty or thirty cash. We will return it tomorrow.” While husband and wife were still talking, Jia Yun had already murmured several times that there was no need to trouble themselves and vanished without a trace. Leaving the Bu couple aside, Jia Yun stormed out of his uncle’s house and retraced his steps. Troubled at heart, he walked on with his head bowed, lost in thought, until he unexpectedly collided headlong with a drunken man and started in alarm. The drunkard cursed, “Damn your mother! Are you blind, barging into me like that?” Jia Yun hastened to dodge away, but the drunkard had already seized him. When he looked into the man’s face, he saw it was none other than his close neighbor Ni Er. This Ni Er was a local rogue who specialized in usurious loans, took protection money from gambling dens, and made a business of brawling and drinking. He was now returning drunk after collecting interest from one of his debtors. Already in a foul temper, he took the collision badly and raised his fist to strike. “Hold your hand, Second Brother!” the other man cried. “It was I who ran into you.” Recognizing a familiar voice, Ni Er opened his drunken eyes and saw Jia Yun. He promptly released him and said with a staggering laugh, “Why, it is Second Master Jia! Forgive me, forgive me. Where are you going at this hour?” “I cannot tell you,” said Jia Yun. “I have just suffered a pointless humiliation.” “Never mind that,” said Ni Er. “Tell me who has wronged you, and I will avenge you. Throughout these streets and alleys, whoever he may be, if anyone offends a neighbor of Ni Er, the Drunken Guardian, I will see his household scattered and himself driven from home!”

p.src: “Second Brother, do not get angry yet,” said Jia Yun. “Listen while I tell you what happened.” He then related the whole affair with Bu Shiren to Ni Er. Ni Er flew into a rage on hearing it. “If he were not your honored uncle, I would curse him in language unfit to hear. He has truly infuriated me! Well, never mind. There is no need for you to fret. I have several taels of silver here; take whatever you need and buy your supplies. But there is one thing: you and I have been neighbors all these years, and although everyone knows that I lend money, you have never once asked me for anything. I do not know whether you despise me as a rogue and fear demeaning yourself, or whether you think me troublesome and my interest too high. If high interest troubles you, I want no interest on this silver, nor need you write a bond. But if you fear demeaning yourself, I dare not lend it to you, and we may each go our own way.” As he spoke, he actually drew a packet of silver from his pouch.

p.src: Jia Yun thought to himself, “Though Ni Er is ordinarily a ruffian and a rogue, he treats different people in different ways and has quite a reputation for chivalry. If I refuse his kindness today, he may feel humiliated and perhaps cause trouble. I had better borrow it and repay him twice as much another day.” Having reached this decision, he smiled and said, “Second Brother, you truly are a gallant fellow. It is not that I have never thought of coming to ask you. But I saw that all those with whom you associated were bold and capable men, and supposed you had no time for powerless nonentities like me. Had I asked you, how could I be sure that you would lend to me? Since you have shown me such generosity today, how could I refuse it? I shall go home, write a proper bond, and bring it to you.” Ni Er laughed heartily. “What a smooth talker you are! But I do not care for what you have just said. If they are truly my friends and associates, how could I lend them money at interest and profit from them? If I lend a man silver in hopes of earning interest from him, then he is no friend or associate of mine. There is no need for any more idle talk. Since you think enough of me to accept it, here are a little over fifteen taels and three mace of silver. Take it and purchase what you need. If you insist on writing some bond, return the silver to me at once, so that I may lend it to people from whom I can expect a profit.” Jia Yun accepted the silver and said with a smile, “Then I shall write nothing. u.src: Jia Yun thought to himself, “Though Ni Er is ordinarily a ruffian and a rogue, he treats different people in different ways and has quite a reputation for chivalry.
If I refuse his kindness today, he may feel humiliated and perhaps cause trouble.
I had better borrow it and repay him twice as much another day.”
Having reached this decision, he smiled and said, “Second Brother, you truly are a gallant fellow. It is not that I have never thought of coming to ask you.
But I saw that all those with whom you associated were bold and capable men, and supposed you had no time for powerless nonentities like me.
Had I asked you, how could I be sure that you would lend to me?
Since you have shown me such generosity today, how could I refuse it? I shall go home, write a proper bond, and bring it to you.”
Ni Er laughed heartily. “What a smooth talker you are!
But I do not care for what you have just said.
If they are truly my friends and associates, how could I lend them money at interest and profit from them?
If I lend a man silver in hopes of earning interest from him, then he is no friend or associate of mine.
There is no need for any more idle talk.

p.src: Now, Jia Yun was greatly surprised by this chance encounter. He reflected that Ni Er did indeed seem a decent sort, yet feared that his drunken generosity might prove fleeting and that the next day he would demand twice as much back. Unsure how he would manage then, Jia Yun remained hesitant. Then another thought came to him: “No matter. Once that business succeeds, I can repay him double.” Having settled this, he went straight to a money shop and had the silver weighed: fifteen taels, three mace, four candareens, and two cash. Seeing that Ni Er had not lied, Jia Yun was more delighted than ever. He put away the silver and returned home, first stopping next door to pass Ni Er’s message to his wife before going into his own house. He found his mother sitting at ease on the kang, twisting thread. When she saw him enter, she asked where he had been all day. Afraid of angering his mother, Jia Yun said nothing of Bu Shiren and merely told her that he had been waiting for Second Uncle Lian at the western mansion. He then asked whether she had eaten. His mother had already eaten and told him that some food had been kept for him. A little maid brought it over for him to eat.

p.src: By then it was already time to light the lamps. Jia Yun finished his meal, made ready for bed, and passed an uneventful night. Early the next morning he rose, washed his face, went out through the southern gate, bought borneol and musk at a large incense shop, and then headed for the Rongguo Mansion. On learning that Jia Lian had gone out, Jia Yun made his way to the rear quarters. At the gate of Jia Lian’s courtyard, he saw several pages sweeping the yard with tall brooms. Suddenly Zhou Rui’s wife emerged from the gate and called to the pages, “Stop sweeping for a moment. Mistress Lian is coming out.” Jia Yun hurried forward and asked with a smile, “Where are you going, Second Aunt?” “The Old Lady has sent for her,” replied Zhou Rui’s wife. “I expect she wants some lengths of cloth cut.” As they spoke, a crowd of attendants appeared escorting Xifeng from the courtyard. Jia Yun knew well that Xifeng delighted in flattery and valued ceremony, so he hastily clasped his hands and stepped forward to greet her with the utmost respect. Without so much as looking directly at him, Xifeng continued walking and merely asked after his mother. “Why does she never come to visit us?” “She has not been very well,” replied Jia Yun. “She often speaks of you and wants to come and see you, Aunt, but she has been unable to.” Xifeng laughed. “What a liar you are! If I had not mentioned her, you would never have told me that she missed me.” Jia Yun laughed. “Only if your nephew had no fear of being struck by lightning would he dare lie before an elder. Only last night she spoke of you, saying how slender and delicate you are, Aunt, and yet how many affairs you have to manage. Fortunately, you possess such extraordinary energy that you arrange everything perfectly; anyone less capable would have been worn out long ago.”

p.src: Xifeng’s face blossomed into smiles. She involuntarily stopped and asked, “What made you and your mother start gossiping about me behind my back?” “There was a reason,” said Jia Yun. “A friend of mine, who is fairly well-off, keeps an incense shop. He had purchased the rank of assistant prefect and was recently appointed somewhere in Yunnan. Since his entire family is going with him, he will no longer keep the shop here. So he settled his accounts and disposed of his stock, paying what was owed, selling cheaply what had to be cleared, and distributing the finer, more valuable goods among his relatives and friends. He happened to give me a quantity of borneol and musk. I discussed it with my mother. If we resold them, not only would they fail to fetch their original price, but who would spend so much silver on such things? Even the wealthiest great families use only a few candareens or mace at a time, and that is extravagant enough. Yet if we wished to give them away, there was no one worthy of using them. It would be a shame to sell them for half of what they are worth. That was why I thought of you, Aunt. In former years I saw you buy these things by the great packetful, Aunt. Quite apart from the needs of the Imperial Consort’s palace this year, with the Dragon Boat Festival approaching, you will naturally require ten times the usual quantity of such aromatics. After much thought, I decided that presenting them to you alone would be fitting and would keep such fine goods from going to waste.” As he spoke, he held up a brocade box.

p.src: Xifeng was just then preparing Dragon Boat Festival gifts and purchasing aromatics and medicines. When Jia Yun appeared with this offering and delivered his speech, she felt both flattered and delighted. She ordered Feng’er, “Take what Brother Yun has brought, carry it home, and hand it to Ping’er.” Then she added, “Seeing how well you understand what is proper, no wonder your uncle often mentions you. He says you speak sensibly and possess sound judgment.” Realizing that her words opened the very path he sought, Jia Yun pressed his advantage and deliberately asked, “So Uncle has spoken of me?” At his question, Xifeng was about to tell him that she meant to put him in charge of some work, but abruptly checked herself. She thought, “If I tell him now, he will think me so greedy for gifts that I promised him a post merely for this little offering of incense. I had better say nothing about it today.” Having decided this, she concealed every word about appointing him to supervise the planting of flowers and trees. After exchanging a few casual remarks, she went on to Grandmother Jia’s quarters. Jia Yun could hardly raise the matter himself, so he had no choice but to go home. Since Baoyu had told him the previous day to wait in the outer study, Jia Yun returned after his meal and went to the Qixia Studio study outside the ceremonial gate leading to Grandmother Jia’s quarters. There he found the two pages Beiming and Chuyao playing chess and quarrelling over possession of a “chariot,” while four or five others—Yinquan, Saohua, Tiaoyun, and Banhe among them—were up under the eaves poking at little sparrows for sport. Jia Yun entered the courtyard, stamped his foot, and cried, “You little monkeys, stop your mischief! I am here.” Only when the pages saw Jia Yun come in did they disperse. Jia Yun went into the room, sat down on a chair, and asked, “Has Second Master Bao not come down?” “He has not come down at all today,” said Beiming. Tell me what you want with Second Master, and I will go scout things out for you.” With that, he went out.

p.src: Jia Yun occupied himself looking at the calligraphy, paintings, and antiques, but after enough time for a meal had passed, no one had yet returned; when he looked for the other pages, he found that they too had all gone off to play. Just as he was growing thoroughly bored, he heard a sweet, tender voice at the doorway call, “Brother!” Jia Yun looked out and saw a maid of sixteen or seventeen, delicately made and neat in appearance. When the maid saw Jia Yun, she drew back and slipped out of sight. At that moment Beiming came along. Seeing the maid by the door, he said, “Good, good! I was just unable to find anyone to carry a message.” On seeing Beiming, Jia Yun also hurried outside and asked how matters stood. Beiming replied, “We have waited all day, but not a soul has come this way. This girl serves in Master Bao’s apartments. Be a good girl and go in with a message: tell him that Second Master Yun from the outer gallery has come.”

p.src: Only then did the maid realize that he was one of the masters of the clan. She no longer avoided him as before, but fixed Jia Yun with two long, intent stares. She heard Jia Yun say, “Never mind all this talk of galleries. Just tell him it is Yun.” After a while, the maid gave a cool little laugh. “If you ask me, Second Master, you had better go home and return tomorrow if you have something to say. If I find a free moment tonight, I shall tell him.” “Why do you say that?” asked Beiming. The maid replied, “He did not take his afternoon nap today, so naturally he will dine early. And he will not come down again this evening. Surely you do not mean to make Second Master wait here and go hungry merely for sport! It would be far better for him to go home and return tomorrow. Even if someone comes back and agrees to carry the message, it will be no use. He will merely say yes—do you really suppose he will deliver it?” Jia Yun was struck by the maid’s crisp and charming way of speaking and wanted to ask her name; but since she belonged to Baoyu’s apartments, he felt it improper to inquire and could only say, “You are right. I shall come again tomorrow.” With that, he started out. Beiming said, “I will fetch some tea. Have a cup before you go, Second Master.” Still walking, Jia Yun looked back and said, “No tea. I have other business to attend to.” Though his lips were speaking, his eyes remained on the maid, who was still standing there.

p.src: Jia Yun went straight home. The next day, as he reached the main gate, he happened upon Xifeng setting out to pay her respects. She had just entered her carriage when she saw him coming, so she ordered someone to stop him and called through the window with a laugh, “Yun, you have quite the nerve to play tricks before my very eyes. No wonder you brought me presents—it turns out you wanted a favor from me. Only yesterday did your uncle tell me that you had asked him for help.” Jia Yun laughed. “Please do not mention my asking Uncle, Aunt. I was regretting it only yesterday. Had I known how matters stood, I would have come straight to you at the outset, and everything would have been settled by now. Who would have thought Uncle could do nothing?” Xifeng laughed. “So that is why nothing came of it there and you sought me out again yesterday.” Jia Yun said, “Aunt, you wrong my filial devotion. I had no such intention at all. Had that been my intention, would I not have asked you yesterday? But now that you know, I mean to leave Uncle aside and must beg you, Aunt, to take pity on me and help me somehow.”

p.src: Xifeng gave a cold laugh. “If you insist on taking the long way round, you make it difficult for me to say anything. Had you told me sooner, what could have prevented it? It is such a trifling matter, yet you have delayed it until now. The garden still needs flowers planted, and I have been unable to think of anyone for the job. Had you come sooner, would it not already have been settled?” Jia Yun laughed. “In that case, Aunt, assign it to me tomorrow.” After a pause, Xifeng said, “I do not think that would be very suitable. Wait until the large contract for fireworks, lamps, and candles comes up in the first month of next year; I shall assign that to you instead.” “Dear Aunt,” said Jia Yun, “please give me this one first. If I truly handle it well, you can give me the other one afterward.” Xifeng laughed. “You certainly know how to cast a long line. Very well. If your uncle had not spoken to me, I would have taken no part in your affairs. I shall return just after my meal. Come around noon to collect the money, and the day after tomorrow you may go in and begin planting the trees.” Having said this, she ordered the fragrant carriage driven on and went straight away.

p.src: Unable to contain his delight, Jia Yun went to Qixia Studio to ask for Baoyu, only to learn that Baoyu had left early that morning for the Prince of Beijing’s residence. Jia Yun sat there vacantly until noon. When he heard that Xifeng had returned, he wrote out a receipt and went to collect the matching authorization tally. Outside the courtyard, he had himself announced. Caiming came out, took only the receipt inside, had the sum and date endorsed upon it, and then handed it back to Jia Yun together with the matching tally. Jia Yun took it and saw that two hundred taels had been authorized. Overjoyed, he turned at once toward the treasury, handed the papers to the clerk receiving tallies and receipts, and collected the silver. He returned home and told his mother, and naturally both mother and son were delighted. At the fifth watch the following morning, Jia Yun first sought out Ni Er and repaid in full the money he had borrowed. Seeing that Jia Yun now had money, Ni Er accepted the exact sum owed; nothing more need be said of that. Jia Yun then took another fifty taels, went out through the west gate, and found the gardener Fang Chun’s house to purchase trees; of this too, no more need be said.

Baoyu started in surprise and asked, “Where were you?
You appeared so suddenly that you gave me a fright.”
Handing him the tea, the maid replied, “I was in the back courtyard. I have only just come in through the rear door of the inner room. Surely you heard my footsteps, Second Master?”

As Baoyu drank his tea, he studied the maid closely. She wore several garments that were neither new nor very old; her luxuriant hair was glossy black and gathered into a knot. She had a longish face and a slender, delicate figure, and looked remarkably pretty and neat.

p.src: After looking at her, Baoyu asked with a smile, “Are you one of the maids in my rooms too?” “Yes,” replied the maid. “If you belong to my rooms, how is it that I don’t know you?” asked Baoyu. At this, the maid gave a cold laugh. “There are plenty you don’t know; I’m hardly the only one. I never bring you tea or water, fetch things, or do any of the conspicuous tasks, so how would you ever come to know me?” “Why don’t you do any of those conspicuous tasks?” asked Baoyu. “That is difficult for me to explain,” said the maid. “But there is one thing I should report to you, Second Master: yesterday someone called Yun came looking for you. But then you went over to the northern mansion again.” She had only just reached this point when Qiuwen and Bihen came in, laughing and chattering. Between them they carried a bucket of water, each holding up her clothes with one hand as they staggered along, splashing water everywhere. The maid hurried forward to take it from them. Qiuwen and Bihen were busy blaming each other. “You’ve wet my skirt,” said one, while the other protested, “You stepped on my shoe.” When someone suddenly came out to take the water, they looked and saw that it was none other than Xiaohong. p.src: Hearing this, Qiuwen spat straight in her face and cursed, “You shameless, low creature! When you were properly told to hurry the water along, you claimed you had something else to do and sent us instead, while you waited here to seize this choice opportunity. Little by little, you are certainly pushing your way to the fore. Do you imagine we can’t keep up with you? Take a look at yourself in the mirror and see whether you are fit to serve tea and water!” Bihen said, “Tomorrow I’ll tell them that whenever tea or water is wanted, or anything has to be carried here or there, none of us need lift a finger; she alone can do it all.” Qiuwen said, “If that is so, we might as well all leave and let her have these rooms to herself.” While the two of them were making a commotion, each talking over the other, an old serving-woman came in with a message from Xifeng: “Tomorrow someone will bring gardeners in to plant trees. You must keep strict order and not leave clothes and skirts drying all over the place. Curtains will be put up all along the artificial hill, so mind you don’t run about carelessly.” Qiuwen asked, “Do you know who will bring the workmen in and oversee them tomorrow?” The old woman replied, “They said something about young Master Yun from the rear gallery.” Qiuwen and Bihen had no idea who that was and went on asking all manner of irrelevant questions. Xiaohong, however, understood as soon as she heard it and knew that he was the man she had seen outside the study the day before. Xiaohong’s surname was actually Lin, and her childhood name was Hongyu. But because the character yu, “jade,” occurred in both Lin Daiyu’s and Baoyu’s names, it was omitted out of respect, and everyone called her Xiaohong, “Little Hong.” Her family had served the Rongguo Mansion for generations, and her parents were now responsible for managing its various houses and fields. Hongyu was sixteen. When servants were assigned to the Prospect Garden, she had been posted to Happy Red Court, which was then a quiet and secluded place. Later, however, when orders were given for the residences to be occupied, this particular one happened to be taken over by Baoyu. Though Hongyu was still an inexperienced maid, her modest share of good looks had filled her with foolish dreams of rising in the world, and she was forever seeking opportunities to display herself before Baoyu. But all those around Baoyu were sharp-tongued and formidable, leaving her no chance to push her way in. Today, just when there seemed to be a glimmer of hope, she had suffered Qiuwen and the others’ spiteful abuse, and half her heart had already turned cold. As she sat brooding, she suddenly heard the old woman mention Jia Yun, and her heart stirred. Still dejected, she returned to her room, lay down on the bed, and pondered in secret, tossing and turning without knowing what to do. Suddenly she heard a low voice outside the window calling, “Hongyu, I found your handkerchief here.” Hongyu hurried outside to look. It was none other than Jia Yun. A blush of embarrassment stole over Hongyu’s face as she asked, “Where did you find it, Second Master?”

p.src: Jia Yun smiled. “Come over here, and I’ll tell you.” As he spoke, he stepped forward to take hold of her. Hongyu hastily turned and ran, but tripped over the threshold and fell. To learn what came of it, read the next chapter.
